content.prompt: Find the range and interquartile range of each data set.

answer.worked:
Ordered data: $3,5,7,7,10,13,15,15,20$.

The median is $10$. Omit it to form the lower half $3,5,7,7$ and upper half $13,15,15,20$.

$$\begin{align*}Q_1&=\frac{5+7}{2}=6\\Q_3&=\frac{15+15}{2}=15\\\text{Range}&=20-3=17\\\text{IQR}&=15-6=9\end{align*}$$

Ordered data: $1,5,5,5,7,7,7,8,8,10$.

Divide into two equal halves: $1,5,5,5,7$ and $7,7,8,8,10$. Each half contains five values, so its third value is its median.

$$\begin{align*}Q_1&=5\\Q_3&=8\\\text{Range}&=10-1=9\\\text{IQR}&=8-5=3\end{align*}$$

Ordered data: $0,4,4,4,6,6,7,9$.

Divide into two equal halves: $0,4,4,4$ and $6,6,7,9$. Average the two middle values of each half.

$$\begin{align*}Q_1&=\frac{4+4}{2}=4\\Q_3&=\frac{6+7}{2}=6.5\\\text{Range}&=9-0=9\\\text{IQR}&=6.5-4=2.5\end{align*}$$

Ordered data: $1,3,5,8,11,13,13,18$.

Divide into two equal halves: $1,3,5,8$ and $11,13,13,18$. Average the two middle values of each half.

$$\begin{align*}Q_1&=\frac{3+5}{2}=4\\Q_3&=\frac{13+13}{2}=13\\\text{Range}&=18-1=17\\\text{IQR}&=13-4=9\end{align*}$$

inlines.text: Find the mean, the mode, the median and the interquartile range of this data set. Give the mean correct to one decimal place.

answer.worked:
The total frequency is $46$. The sum of the data values is
$$\begin{align*}\sum fx&=0\times5+1\times2+2\times0+3\times7+4\times1+5\times8\\&\quad+6\times4+7\times6+8\times0+9\times2+10\times11\\\sum fx&=261\\\overline{x}&=\frac{261}{46}\\\overline{x}&\approx5.7\quad\text{(1 decimal place)}\end{align*}$$
The greatest frequency is $11$, belonging to value $10$, so the mode is $10$.

The cumulative frequencies for values $0$ to $10$ are $5,7,7,14,15,23,27,33,33,35,46$. The 23rd value is $5$ and the 24th is $6$.
$$\begin{align*}\text{Median}&=\frac{5+6}{2}\\\text{Median}&=5.5\end{align*}$$
Each half contains $23$ values. The lower quartile is the 12th value overall, and the upper quartile is the 35th value overall.
$$\begin{align*}Q_1&=3\\Q_3&=9\\\text{IQR}&=9-3\\\text{IQR}&=6\end{align*}$$

answer.worked:
There are 20 heights, so the median is the average of the 10th and 11th values, $161$ and $162$.
$$\begin{align*}\text{Median}&=\frac{161+162}{2}\\\text{Median}&=161.5\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$

$$\begin{align*}Q_1&=\frac{151+152}{2}\\Q_1&=151.5\text{ cm}\\Q_3&=\frac{172+176}{2}\\Q_3&=174\text{ cm}\\\text{IQR}&=174-151.5\\\text{IQR}&=22.5\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$

inlines.text: The following figures are the amounts a family spent on food each week for 13 weeks.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Find the median, upper quartile and lower quartile.

answer.worked:
In ascending order, the amounts in dollars are:
$$139,141,143,143,147,148,149,150,152,152,155,158,158.$$
There are 13 values, so the median is the seventh value, $\$149$. Omit this value when dividing the data into two groups of six. Average the two middle values in each group.
$$\begin{align*}Q_3&=\frac{152+155}{2}\\Q_3&=153.50\\Q_1&=\frac{143+143}{2}\\Q_1&=143\end{align*}$$
Thus the upper quartile is $\$153.50$ and the lower quartile is $\$143$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Find the interquartile range of the amounts spent.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\text{IQR}&=Q_3-Q_1\\\text{IQR}&=153.50-143\\\text{IQR}&=10.50\end{align*}$$
The interquartile range is $\$10.50$.

content.prompt: The median is always between the two quartiles. Is the mean always between the two quartiles? If not, give an example of seven whole numbers where the mean is above the upper quartile and an example where the mean is below the lower quartile.

answer.short:
No. Sample answers:

Above the upper quartile: $1,1,1,2,2,3,18$, with mean $4$ and upper quartile $3$.

Below the lower quartile: $0,7,7,7,7,7,7$, with mean $6$ and lower quartile $7$.
answer.worked:
No. For seven ordered values, omit the fourth value when finding the quartiles; the lower and upper quartiles are the second and sixth values.

For $1,1,1,2,2,3,18$:
$$\begin{align*}Q_1&=1\\Q_3&=3\\\overline{x}&=\frac{1+1+1+2+2+3+18}{7}\\\overline{x}&=4\end{align*}$$
The mean $4$ is above the upper quartile $3$.

For $0,7,7,7,7,7,7$:
$$\begin{align*}Q_1&=7\\Q_3&=7\\\overline{x}&=\frac{0+7+7+7+7+7+7}{7}\\\overline{x}&=6\end{align*}$$
The mean $6$ is below the lower quartile $7$.

classification.difficultyReason: Express deviations algebraically and connect their sum to the defining identity that the total equals the number of values times the mean. Generalising to an arbitrary data set requires symbolic reasoning, scaffolded by the three-value proof in part a.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Prove that the sum of the deviations for the data set $a,b,c$ is zero.

answer.short:
$(a-\bar{x})+(b-\bar{x})+(c-\bar{x})=0$.

Substitute $\bar{x}=\dfrac{a+b+c}{3}$ into the sum of the deviations.
answer.worked:
The mean is $\bar{x}=\dfrac{a+b+c}{3}$. Therefore,
$$\begin{aligned}(a-\bar{x})+(b-\bar{x})+(c-\bar{x})&=(a+b+c)-3\bar{x}\\(a-\bar{x})+(b-\bar{x})+(c-\bar{x})&=(a+b+c)-3\left(\frac{a+b+c}{3}\right)\\(a-\bar{x})+(b-\bar{x})+(c-\bar{x})&=0.\end{aligned}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Prove that the sum of the deviations of any data set is zero.

answer.short:
$(x_1-\bar{x})+\cdots+(x_n-\bar{x})=0$.

The sum of the data values equals $n\bar{x}$, so subtracting the mean from each of the $n$ values gives a total of zero.
answer.worked:
Let the data values be $x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n$. Their mean is $\bar{x}=\dfrac{x_1+x_2+\cdots+x_n}{n}$. Therefore,
$$\begin{aligned}(x_1-\bar{x})+\cdots+(x_n-\bar{x})&=(x_1+\cdots+x_n)-n\bar{x}\\(x_1-\bar{x})+\cdots+(x_n-\bar{x})&=(x_1+\cdots+x_n)-n\left(\frac{x_1+\cdots+x_n}{n}\right)\\(x_1-\bar{x})+\cdots+(x_n-\bar{x})&=0.\end{aligned}$$

children.label: a
children.prompt: For each set of data, calculate the mean and the standard deviation.

answer.worked:
Each distribution is symmetric about $6.5$, so each mean is $6.5$. Using $\sigma=\sqrt{\frac{\sum f(x-\bar{x})^2}{\sum f}}$:

$$\begin{align*}\sigma_{\mathrm{i}}&=\sqrt{\frac{3(2.5^2+1.5^2+0.5^2+0.5^2+1.5^2+2.5^2)}{18}}\\\sigma_{\mathrm{i}}&=\sqrt{\frac{35}{12}}\\\sigma_{\mathrm{i}}&\approx1.71\end{align*}$$

$$\begin{align*}\sigma_{\mathrm{ii}}&=\sqrt{\frac{2(2.5^2)+4(1.5^2)+6(0.5^2)}{12}}\\\sigma_{\mathrm{ii}}&=\sqrt{\frac{23}{12}}\\\sigma_{\mathrm{ii}}&\approx1.38\end{align*}$$

$$\begin{align*}\sigma_{\mathrm{iii}}&=\sqrt{\frac{6(2.5^2)+4(1.5^2)+2(0.5^2)}{12}}\\\sigma_{\mathrm{iii}}&=\sqrt{\frac{47}{12}}\\\sigma_{\mathrm{iii}}&\approx1.98\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Add 5 onto each data item in each of i, ii and iii and state the mean and standard deviation of each new set of data.

answer.worked:
Adding $5$ increases each mean by $5$. Each value's deviation from its new mean is unchanged, so each standard deviation is unchanged.

$$\bar{x}_{\mathrm{new}}=6.5+5=11.5.$$

Thus the standard deviations for i, ii and iii are respectively $\sqrt{35/12}\approx1.71$, $\sqrt{23/12}\approx1.38$ and $\sqrt{47/12}\approx1.98$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Multiply each data item in each of i, ii and iii by 2 and state the mean and standard deviation of each new set of data.

answer.worked:
Multiplying every value by $2$ doubles the mean and every deviation from the mean, so it doubles the standard deviation. Use the unrounded standard deviations.

$$\bar{x}_{\mathrm{new}}=2\times6.5=13.$$

$$\begin{align*}\sigma_{\mathrm{i,new}}&=2\sqrt{\frac{35}{12}}\approx3.42\\\sigma_{\mathrm{ii,new}}&=2\sqrt{\frac{23}{12}}\approx2.77\\\sigma_{\mathrm{iii,new}}&=2\sqrt{\frac{47}{12}}\approx3.96\end{align*}$$

inlines.text: The number of times 35 randomly chosen Year 10 students go online in the course of a school day was recorded. The results are shown in the frequency table below.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Calculate the mean number of times students in this random sample go online.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\sum fx&=0(8)+1(3)+2(5)+3(6)+4(7)+5(5)+6(0)+7(1)\\\sum fx&=91\\\overline{x}&=\frac{91}{35}\\\overline{x}&=2.6\end{align*}$$
The mean is $2.6$ times.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Find the standard deviation of the number of times students go online, correct to two decimal places.

answer.worked:
Using the frequency-weighted squared deviations:
$$\begin{align*}\sum f(x-2.6)^2&=8(6.76)+3(2.56)+5(0.36)+6(0.16)\\&\quad+7(1.96)+5(5.76)+0(11.56)+1(19.36)\\\sum f(x-2.6)^2&=126.4\\\sigma&=\sqrt{\frac{126.4}{35}}\\\sigma&\approx1.90\end{align*}$$
The standard deviation is $1.90$ times, correct to two decimal places.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Find the range of times online that lie within one standard deviation of the mean.

answer.worked:
Using the unrounded standard deviation:
$$\begin{align*}\overline{x}-\sigma&=2.6-\sqrt{\frac{126.4}{35}}\approx0.70\\\overline{x}+\sigma&=2.6+\sqrt{\frac{126.4}{35}}\approx4.50\end{align*}$$
The whole-number counts in this interval are $1,2,3,4$. Thus the range is $1$ to $4$ times, inclusive.

children.label: d
children.prompt: If every student in this sample went online one more time than what was recorded, determine the effect on the mean and standard deviation.

answer.short: The mean increases by $1$, from $2.6$ to $3.6$ times. The standard deviation remains $1.90$ times.
answer.worked:
Adding $1$ to every value also adds $1$ to the mean, so the new mean is $2.6+1=3.6$ times.

Each deviation is unchanged because $(x+1)-(\overline{x}+1)=x-\overline{x}$. Therefore the standard deviation remains $\sqrt{126.4/35}\approx1.90$ times.

spec.mathematics: Horizontal ticks 30–46 in steps of 1; vertical ticks 140–190 in steps of 5. The supplied line is represented by h=2.5t+72.5 over approximately 30.9≤t≤45.2.
spec.answerVisibility: Observations and fitted line are permanent givens. The equation and selected calculation points are not printed on the question graph.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Determine the equation of the line of best fit.

answer.short:
$h=2.5t+72.5$, where $h$ is height in centimetres and $t$ is tibia length in centimetres.

Use two well-separated points on the supplied line to find its gradient.
answer.worked:
Let $t$ be tibia length and $h$ be height, both in centimetres. Read approximately $(31,150)$ and $(45,185)$ from the fitted line.

$$\begin{aligned}m&=\frac{185-150}{45-31}\\m&=\frac{35}{14}\\m&=2.5\end{aligned}$$

Using point–gradient form:

$$\begin{aligned}h-150&=2.5(t-31)\\h-150&=2.5t-77.5\\h&=2.5t+72.5\end{aligned}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Use the equation to predict the height of a Year 10 female with tibia length of 44 cm.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}h&=2.5(44)+72.5\\h&=110+72.5\\h&=182.5\end{aligned}$$

The predicted height is $182.5\text{ cm}$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Use the equation to predict the tibia length of a 145 cm tall Year 10 female.

answer.short:
$29\text{ cm}$.

Substitute the height and solve for tibia length.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}145&=2.5t+72.5\\72.5&=2.5t\\t&=\frac{72.5}{2.5}\\t&=29\end{aligned}$$

The predicted tibia length is $29\text{ cm}$.

children.label: d
children.prompt: Are these predictions examples of interpolation or extrapolation? Explain your answer.

answer.short: (b) Interpolation: $44\text{ cm}$ is within the observed tibia lengths. (c) Extrapolation: $145\text{ cm}$ is below the observed heights.
answer.worked:
In (b), the given tibia length of $44\text{ cm}$ lies within the observed range of approximately $31$–$45\text{ cm}$, so the prediction is interpolation.

In (c), the given height of $145\text{ cm}$ lies below the observed height range of approximately $148$–$185\text{ cm}$, so the prediction is extrapolation.

entries.description:
In previous books in this series, we have looked at the measures of central tendency, such as the mean and the median.

In this chapter, we discuss two measurements of spread – the interquartile range and standard deviation. The representation of numerical data by boxplots is also introduced.

In our study of statistics up to now, we have often associated one measurement with an item. For example, the height of each person in a class, the number of possessions obtained by a player in a football match or the number of marks obtained by a student in a test.

In the last two sections of this chapter, we look at associating a pair of numbers with an item, for example, the height and weight of a person or the age and salary of an employee. This is called bivariate data.

When a measurement is collected or recorded at successive intervals of time, it is referred to as time-series data. This type of bivariate data is also introduced in this chapter.

entries.description:
The interquartile range(IQR) measures the spread of the middle 50% of the data in an ordered data set.
We use the interquartile range to see how closely the data are grouped around the median. When we calculate the interquartile range, we organise the data into quartiles, each containing 25% of the data. The word ‘quartile’ is related to ‘quarter’.
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone definitions and explanation, retained as taught-method evidence.

entries.description:
Olivia has been playing Sudoku on the internet. Her last 11 games were all rated ‘diabolical’, and her times, correct to the nearest minute and arranged in ascending order, were:
8, 12, 14, 14, 16, 18, 19, 19, 25, 78, 523
The range of these times is 523 − 8 = 515.
entries.exclusionReason: Supplied demonstration data and calculation; no student task is printed.

entries.description:
Clearly the range does not give a clear picture of Olivia’s considerable skills, because the last two times, 78 and 523, are outliers. An outlier is a single data value far away from the rest of the data. That is, it is much larger or much smaller than all of the other values. Outliers have a huge influence on the value of both the mean and the range. (In fact, the time of 78 minutes occurred when Olivia left the game running over dinner, and the time of 523 minutes occurred when Olivia left the game running overnight.)
Because of situations like this, the interquartile range is often a better measure of the spread of the data than the range. Here is the procedure for finding it.
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone explanation and demonstration context; not a practice question.

entries.description:
Step 1: Find the median. Divide the data into two equal groups. Omit the median (middle value) if there is an odd number of values. In Olivia’s case, there are 11 values so, omitting the median 18, the two groups of 5 are:
8, 12, 14, 14, 16 and 19, 19, 25, 78, 523
entries.exclusionReason: Supplied teaching procedure and working, retained as taught-method evidence.

entries.description: Step 2: The lower quartile is the median of the lower set of values. In Olivia’s case, the lower quartile is 14.
entries.exclusionReason: Supplied teaching procedure and result; not a practice question.

entries.description: Step 3: The upper quartile is the median of the upper set of values. In Olivia’s case, the upper quartile is 25.
entries.exclusionReason: Supplied teaching procedure and result; not a practice question.

entries.description:
Step 4: The interquartile range is the difference between the two quartiles. In Olivia’s case:
Interquartile range = 25 − 14
                    = 11
Thus, the middle 50% of Olivia’s times have a spread of 11 minutes.

entries.description:
The mean of a data set is a measure of its centre. The mean is calculated by adding together all the data values and then dividing the resulting sum by the number of data values.
Mean = (sum of values)/(number of values)
A more common name for the mean is ‘average’. We use the symbol x̄ to denote the mean.
For a set of data x₁, x₂, x₃, …, xₙ,
x̄ = (x₁ + x₂ + x₃ + … + xₙ)/n

The standard deviation of a set of data is a measure of how far the data values are spread out from the mean. The difference between each data item and the mean is called the deviation of the data value. The sum of the deviations is zero, which will be proved in question 10 of Exercise 18D.

entries.description:
• The mean of a set of data is denoted by \(\bar{x}\).
• The standard deviation of a data set is a measure of spread and is denoted by the Greek letter \(\sigma\).
• There are two formulas for the standard deviation.
\[\sigma=\sqrt{\frac{(x_1-\bar{x})^2+(x_2-\bar{x})^2+(x_3-\bar{x})^2+\ldots+(x_n-\bar{x})^2}{n}},\] when the data is in a list.
\[\sigma=\sqrt{\frac{f_1(x_1-\bar{x})^2+f_2(x_2-\bar{x})^2+f_3(x_3-\bar{x})^2+\ldots+f_s(x_s-\bar{x})^2}{f_1+f_2+\ldots+f_s}},\] when the data is in a frequency table.

entries.description:
Many calculators and spreadsheets have a built-in facility for calculating the standard deviation of a set of data.
To save time, we recommend using this facility for all but the simplest data sets. In particular, if \(\bar{x}\) is not an integer, then calculating \(\sigma\) is very tedious.
It should be noted that in this book we calculate the standard deviation by dividing the sum of the squares of the deviations by \(n\), the number of data items, and taking the square root. There is also another type of standard deviation that is obtained by dividing the sum of the squares of the deviations by \(n-1\), and taking the square root. Many calculators offer both versions. Sometimes they are denoted by symbols such as \(\sigma_n\) and \(\sigma_{n-1}\). In this book, we only use \(\sigma_n\).

A remarkable result known as Chebyshev’s inequality states that, for any set of data, if we take an interval between \bar{x}-k\sigma and \bar{x}+k\sigma, then all values can lie outside this interval for 0<k≤1, but for k>1, at most 1/k² of the data can lie outside this interval.
So, for example, taking k=2, not more than 1/4 of the data can be outside this interval.
So at least 75% of the data must lie inside this interval.

entries.description: You may have noticed that creating a line of best fit by eye is prone to variation and discrepancy. This is not desirable if we need to be consistent and accurate with fitting a line to data. Fortunately, there are several alternative approaches to drawing a line of best fit. The approach commonly used is called the least squares method.

entries.description:
• Drawing a line of best fit by eye consists of tracing the trend of the scatter plot with a straight line, ensuring that there are roughly equal numbers of points above and below the line, with distance of points from the line taken into account.
